newsitem.title: USA: New U.S. stock rules likely to hurt dealer profits.
newsitem.headline: New U.S. stock rules likely to hurt dealer profits.

text.p: Wall Street firms making markets in Nasdaq stocks will find the business less profitable under new rules imposed by the Securities and Exchange Commission, experts and market participants said.
But small investors will find it costs less to trade.
"It sounds good," said a private investor who did not want to be identified. "I think it's very positive."
"We're going to see a narrowing of the spreads (between dealers' buying and selling prices)," said Perrin Long, an independent analyst.

"A narrowing of the spreads which is not accompanied by sharply higher volume obviously means lower profits if the firms who are market makers are unable to reduce their day-to-day operating costs in line wtih the narrowing of the spreads," said Long. The independent analyst tracks the securities industry.

The new rules go into effect for all exchange-listed stocks and for the 1,000 most liquid Nasdaq stocks 120 days after a comment period. The rules will be phased in for an additional 3,500 Nasdaq stocks over the following six months.
All remaining securities on the National Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation system will be covered on the first anniversary of the adoption of the rules.
Nasdaq officials and some Wall Street firms were quick to praise the new rules.
"These rules provide a solid framework that will help level the playing field for individual investors," said Alfred Berkeley, president of the Nasdaq Stock Market.
"These rules are designed to increase transparency and enhance limit order protection in the Nasdaq market," said a spokesman for Merrill Lynch & Co Inc.
The Merrill Lynch spokesman said the changes "will benefit investors and issuers alike."
He added, "Merrill Lynch remains fully committed to Nasdaq and supports the ongoing process of change to strengthen and improve the market."
Merrill Lynch makes markets in about 900 Nasdaq stocks.

In the Nasdaq market, customers buy stocks from a dealer and sell stocks to a dealer. The dealer makes a market, displaying a bid price at which he buys stock and an "offer" or "ask" price at which he sells. The difference is the "spread," or gross profit on the transaction.
Nasdaq trading practices began to come under scrutiny after the 1987 stock market crash. At that time, there was widespread criticism that dealers in the market were not answering their telephones.

Over the years, a number of academic researchers have published research alleging that the Nasdaq spreads were too big. Nasdaq market makers defended their practices, arguing among other things that some stocks do not trade actively and deserve wide spreads. In the Nasdaq market, dealers have to maintain an inventory in the stocks in which they advertise their presence as market makers.

The private investor who said he was pleased with the new rules said small investors, if they want to take advantage of the new rules, must learn to tell their brokers they want to place limit orders, specifying the price at which they want to buy or sell. He added that in cases were a stock is making a big move up or down a market order may be a better strategy.

Under the new rules, customers' limit orders with better buying and selling prices than the current quote must be displayed. Nasdaq is pushing for approval of a new technology called NAqcess which will allow matching of limit orders to buy and sell.
